newsitem.title: FRANCE: US, France said overcoming Zaire differences.
newsitem.headline: US, France said overcoming Zaire differences.

text.p: The United States and European allies, overcoming past differences, have agreed to back a United Nations plan to resolve the crisis in Zaire, the French Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.

Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told reporters that senior diplomats from the United States and six European Union countries agreed in informal talks in Paris on Tuesday to call for a ceasefire in Zaire and respect for the central African country's territorial integrity.

"All participants reaffirmed unambiguously their adhesion to the principles that must guide the international community in helping restore peace and stability in Zaire -- the very guidelines that inspire the five-point peace plan....unanimously agreed by the U.N. Security Council," he said.

Amid bombing raids on rebel-held towns in eastern Zaire, the Security Council called on Tuesday for an immediate ceasefire, withdrawal of all foreign forces including mercenaries, respect for the territorial integrity of Zaire and its neighbours, and an international peace conference.
"We strongly hope these converging efforts will rapidly bear fruit," Rummelhardt said.

He said the agreement between the directors of Africa departments at the foreign ministries of the United States, France, Germany, Britain Belgium, Spain and the Netherlands, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, showed that disagreements had been overcome.

French officials say Washington appears to have come around to their view that a collapse and possible break-up of Zaire could destabilise the whole of central Africa and would not be in U.S. interests.
Zaire has accused Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of backing the rebels, led by ethnic Tutsis. All three countries reject the accusations.

The United States and France squabbled last year over a U.N.-sponsored multinational force to protect refugees caught in the Zaire fighting, mostly Hutus from Rwanda. The mission was cancelled after most refugees returned home on their own.

France backed the previous Hutu-led Rwandan government. Analysts said Paris believed that Washington, which is closely linked to Rwanda and Uganda, was trying to edge it out of the last region where it still wields influence from its colonial past.

A joint statement issued after Tuesday's Paris meeting said participants favoured "talks, implementation of the electoral process and an international conference, under the auspices of the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity, for peace, security and development in the region of the Great Lakes."
It said they agreed to support and work closely with U.N. special envoy Mohammed Sahnoun.
Zaire said the Security Council resolution was "a timid advance" and should have condemned aggressors in the conflict.
